f318d2fc91.q: Why do 91% of U.S. family business leaders expect only 36% of family members to hold senior executive positions over the next decade according to KPMG?
f318d2fc91.a: According to a KPMG report released August 27, while 91% of surveyed U.S. family business leaders are confident in the next generation's ability to serve as owners and board members, only 36% expect family members to hold most senior executive positions over the next decade. This reflects a trend where family ownership is increasingly becoming separated from day-to-day management.
f318d2fc91.e: Why Some Family Businesses Last Fifty Years and Others Die in One Generation
f318d2fc91.rq: Ownership can be inherited. Leadership has to be earned.

1a6a2c5ff6.q: What are the three major obstacles to succession identified in Deloitte's 2026 Global Family Business Study?
1a6a2c5ff6.a: According to Deloitte's 2026 Global Family Business Study, the three major obstacles to succession are: 35% cite next generation inexperience or lack of qualifications, 33% cite difficulty finding a suitable successor, and 32% identify existing leadership's reluctance to give up control. The last number deserves attention because sometimes the biggest obstacle is the current generation refusing to let go.

c70a23633e.q: What is the distinction between inherited ownership and earned leadership in family business succession?
c70a23633e.a: Ownership can be inherited, but leadership has to be earned. Being a family member and being a qualified business leader are two entirely different things. A family member might be wonderful, intelligent, and hardworking, but that does not automatically make them qualified to manage people, make financial decisions, negotiate with customers, understand operations, or lead the company through difficult times.

d8f2c623ef.q: Why is separating family business ownership from day-to-day management considered essential for long-term succession?
d8f2c623ef.a: A family can retain ownership and appoint qualified professional executives without requiring family members to manage the company. Major companies like Pepsi, Coca-Cola, and Chipotle do not have family people running the business. The goal should be continuity and performance, not simply keeping every important title in the family. Sometimes this approach is the smartest way to preserve the business.
